extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, writers, and publishers working in American English
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive punctuation and typographic rules for preparing text for publication, covering periods, quotation marks, colons, semicolons, commas, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, and word divisions. Aimed at editorial decision-making and consistent copy preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 124. No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: 125. Omit period after certain headings and lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads; after centered headlines; after side-heads set in separate lines; after cut-in heads; after box-heads in tables; and after superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence; after date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 50 for related material.

rubrics_metrics.name: 126. Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside the quotation marks; and inside the parentheses when the matter inclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam.' Put the period inside the quotation marks. When parentheses form part of preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: 127. Exclamation point usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided showing emphatic/ironical uses: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' 'Good!' he cried; 'How funny this seems!'

rubrics_metrics.name: 128. Exclamation point placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is placed inside the quotation marks when part of the quotation; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations in rule 127.

rubrics_metrics.name: 129. Interrogation point (question mark) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query, or to express a doubt. Indirect questions, however, should not be followed by an interrogation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' Indirect question: He asked whether he was ill. (No question mark.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 130. Interrogation point placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point should be placed inside the quotation marks only when it is a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The question: 'Who is who, and what is what?' Were you ever in 'Tsintsinnati'?

rubrics_metrics.name: 131. Colon: primary uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon is used to mark a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period; commonly used (i) to emphasize a close connection in thought between two clauses each of which forms a complete sentence; (2) to separate a clause grammatically complete from a second which contains an illustration or amplification; (3) to introduce a formal statement, an extract, a speech in a dialogue, etc., unless preceded by a conjunction immediately connecting it with what goes before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the quotation of a clause in the middle of a sentence use a comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: 132. Colon substitutes for words like 'namely' or 'for example'
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon often takes the place of an implied 'namely,' 'as follows,' 'for instance,' or similar phrase. Where such a word or phrase is used, it should be followed by a colon if what follows consists of one or more grammatically complete clauses; otherwise by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrasting colon vs comma when followed by clauses vs phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 133. Colon after salutatory and introductory phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter, and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: My dear Mr. Brown:; Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:

rubrics_metrics.name: 134. Colon in Scripture and time references
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: 135. Colon between place and publisher in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between the place of publication and the publisher's name in literary and bibliographical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), 11, 97.

rubrics_metrics.name: 136. Colon placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He writes under the head of 'Notes and Comments': 'Many a man can testify...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 137. Semicolon: general use
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous illustrative examples showing semicolons connecting independent but related clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 138. Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations use a semicolon between the different links if these consist of more than a few words closely connected, and especially if individual clauses contain any punctuation mark of less value than a period, or an exclamation or interrogation point, yet are intimately joined one with the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating use in long or parenthetical enumeration items.

rubrics_metrics.name: 139. Semicolon in Scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references a semicolon is used to separate passages containing chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 140. Semicolon placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General placement rule similar to other terminal punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 141. Comma: general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples illustrating subtle uses to preserve clarity and avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 142. Comma separating proper nouns of different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 143. Oxford/serial comma rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and,' 'or,' and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; or all the links in a series of greater length, or where each individual link consists of several words; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tom, Dick, and Harry; either copper, silver, or gold. Exception: omit in brief close-knit phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 144. Comma with clauses introduced by conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions like 'and,' 'but,' 'if,' 'while,' 'as,' 'whereas,' 'since,' 'because,' 'when,' 'after,' 'although,' especially if a change of subject takes place; but do not use a comma where the preceding clause is not logically complete without them or in brief, close-welded phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples showing when commas are and are not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 145. Comma with introductory and parenthetical connective words
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions, adverbs, connective particles, or phrases such as 'now,' 'then,' 'however,' 'indeed,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' etc., should be followed by a comma when standing at the beginning of a sentence or clause to introduce an inference or an explanation, and should be placed between commas when wedged into the middle of a sentence or clause to mark off a distinct break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also lists exceptions where comma may be omitted for close connections (e.g., 'Therefore I say...'; 'He was therefore unable...').

rubrics_metrics.name: 146. Comma before 'rather' (preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is preferably omitted before 'rather' in expressions like 'measured in this way rather than by...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic preference guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 147. Commas between multiple adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, it should not be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the admirable political institutions of the country'; 'a handsome, wealthy young man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 148. Commas with participial clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially such as contain an explanation of the main clause, should usually be set off by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him'; 'Exhausted by a hard day's work, he slept like a stone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 149. Comma before 'not' introducing antithetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 150. Use of commas vs dashes for interpolations
rubrics_metrics.description: For parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use the two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrasting commas and dashes; cross-reference to rules 175 and 167.

rubrics_metrics.name: 151. Comma to separate identical or closely similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words, even if the sense or grammatical construction does not require such separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whatever is, is good'; 'What he was, is not known'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 152. Commas with qualifying or delimiting adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though perfectly logical, conclusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 153. Commas between coordinate clauses modifying another clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more co-ordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating construction: 'a shallow body of water connected with, but well protected from, the open sea.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 154. Comma to separate numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers (e.g., in dates and page-number contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention'; 'November 1, 1905.' See rule 160 for related time conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 155. Comma to indicate omitted words
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples with parallel constructions: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two; in Indiana, thirteen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 156. Comma before brief quotations or maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression, when brief, should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 157. Comma before 'of' with residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position (e.g., 'Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.'), except when the place-name has become practically part of the person's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: Clement of Alexandria, Philip of Anjou, King Edward of England.

rubrics_metrics.name: 158. No comma between consecutive pages; use en-dash
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma between consecutive pages in literary references, but use the en-dash; an exception may be made for scriptural references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pp. 4, 7-8, 10; Ezra 5:7-8 (or Ezra 5:7, 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: 159. Comma after digits indicating thousands
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except when used as a date or in a page-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,276; 10,419; January, 1909; p. 2461. Note: some journals omit comma with four figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 160. Comma separating month and year
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year, and similar time divisions, by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906. Note that some journals do not use this comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: 161. Omit comma in signatures/address blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given of signature formatting showing omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: 162. Comma placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule; consistent with American-style punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 163. Apostrophe for contractions and omitted figures
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas, '96.

rubrics_metrics.name: 164. Forming possessive case with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s (varies by ending and syllable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe; Themistocles' era.

rubrics_metrics.name: 165. Apostrophe in plurals of numerals and rare coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals, and of rare or artificial noun-coinages, is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; rules vary for proper nouns ending in sibilant and for monosyllabic vs multisyllabic names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; the three R's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; exceptions and variants noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 166. Dash: denote sudden break or abrupt change
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash is used to denote 'a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous literary examples; shows rhetorical emphasis uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 167. Use dashes for independent parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided; cross-reference to parentheses rule 176 and comma/dash distinctions at 150.

rubrics_metrics.name: 168. Dash to introduce emphatic explanatory clause repeating phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 169. Dash where 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of enumerative insertions set off by dashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 170. Dash before final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final — summarizing — clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example showing final summarizing clause preceded by dash.

rubrics_metrics.name: 171. Dash following a line-set word followed by paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs, at the beginning of each of which it is implied, should be followed by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I recommend — 1. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 172. Dash with side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows side-head followed by em-dash then text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 173. Dash for ranges and connecting numbers/words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in place of the word 'to' connecting two words or numbers (distinguish en-dash for month ranges and em-dash for breaks); rules for omitting hundreds in consecutive numbers and for B.C. dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May–July, 1906 (en-dash); May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em-dash); pp. 3-7 (en-dash); advice on repeating hundreds in B.C. citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 174. Dash before citation after a full quoted sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title of work, or both) following a direct quotation, consisting of at least one complete sentence, in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows quoted sentence followed by em-dash then reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 175. Restriction on dash usage with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of incorrect combinations: 'Dear Sir: — I have...' is incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 176. Parentheses for enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text. If such divisions are paragraphed, follow typographic conventions: single parenthesis with lower-case italic letter; period with figures and capital roman letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives recommended hierarchical scheme of A., I., 1., a), (i), (a), a), β) etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 177. Limited use of parentheses for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise from the use of less distinctive marks, or unless the content of the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show when parentheses can be used vs dash or comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: 178. Brackets: purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for each use are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 179. Brackets for 'To be continued' notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Such phrases as 'To be continued' at the end, and 'Continued from...' at the beginning of articles, chapters, etc., should be placed between brackets, centered, and set in italics and in type reduced in size in accordance with rules governing reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320] [To be concluded]

rubrics_metrics.name: 180. Ellipses: indicate omission and typography
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission, from a quotation, of one or more words not essential to the idea, and to indicate illegible words or lacunae. For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence four periods, separated by a space (en-quad), should ordinarily be used, except in very narrow measures. If the preceding line ends in a point, that point should not be included in the four. When whole paragraphs or lines in poetry are omitted, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads, but periods should not extend beyond the length of the longest type-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of ellipsis use in prose and poetry provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 181. Ellipsis treated as part of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as a part of the citation; consequently should be inclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to bracket/quotation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 182. Hyphen at line breaks and between many compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word carried to the next line and between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See section on divisions for hyphenation at line end.

rubrics_metrics.name: 183. Hyphenate compound adjectives preceding a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: so-called Croesus, well-known author, first-class investment; when set in capitals or one component contains more than one word, use en-dash (e.g., FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR). Do not hyphenate adverb + -ly combinations or adjectives following the noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: 184. Hyphenate objective compound nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate, as a rule, nouns formed by the combination of two nouns standing in objective relation to each other (one component derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, office-holder; exceptions: lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader.

rubrics_metrics.name: 185. Hyphen with present participle forming nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united (i) with a noun to form a new noun with different meaning, or (2) with a preposition used absolutely to form a noun, should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, walking-stick.

rubrics_metrics.name: 186. Hyphenation rules for compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, compounds of 'book,' 'house,' 'mill,' 'room,' 'shop,' and 'work' should be printed as one compact word when the prefixed noun contains only one syllable; hyphenated when it contains two; printed as two separate words when it contains three or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples grouped by prefix syllable length: handbook, schoolbook; pocket-book, story-book; reference book.

rubrics_metrics.name: 187. Hyphenate compounds of maker/dealer and dual-occupation nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker,' 'dealer,' and other words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated; likewise nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; soldier-statesman, poet-artist Rossetti. Some short words are exceptions (bookmaker).

rubrics_metrics.name: 188. Hyphenation of store compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: 189. Compounds of 'fellow' always hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: 190. Hyphenate kinship compound nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'father,' 'mother,' 'brother,' 'sister,' 'daughter,' 'parent,' and 'foster' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but: fatherland), mother-tongue, foster-son.

rubrics_metrics.name: 191. Hyphenate 'great-' in descent compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great,' indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: 192. Hyphenate compounds of 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: 193. Compounds of 'skin' formatting by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with one-syllable words are printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: 194. Hyphenate compounds of 'master'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).

rubrics_metrics.name: 195. Hyphenate compounds of 'god'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'god' use a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god.

rubrics_metrics.name: 196. Hyphen with fractions like 'half-' and 'quarter-'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half,' 'quarter,' etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, quarter-mile.

rubrics_metrics.name: 197. Hyphenation with prefixes semi-/demi-/bi-/tri- usually omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Semi,' 'demi,' 'bi,' 'tri,' etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, biweekly; exceptions: semi-centennial, demi-révêlo (long/unusual formations).

rubrics_metrics.name: 198. Compounds of 'self' are hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'self' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 199. 'Fold' combinations formatting by syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are printed as one word if the number contains only one syllable; if it contains more, as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: 200. '-like' adjectives: hyphenation by noun syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixation of 'like' to a noun are usually printed as one word if the noun contains only one syllable (except when ending in l); if it contains more (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: 201. Hyphenate title components like 'vice-' 'ex-' 'elect'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vice,' 'ex-,' 'elect,' 'general,' and 'lieutenant,' constituting parts of titles, should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 202. Hyphenate 'by-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'by-' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: 203. Hyphenation with prefixes co-, pre-, re- when followed by same vowel
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-,' 'pre-,' and 're-,' when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, take a hyphen; but, as a rule, they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstal. Note exceptions with proper names, unusual formations, or where omission changes meaning (re-cover vs recover).

rubrics_metrics.name: 204. Omit hyphen in certain closed compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen from 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'viewpoint,' 'standpoint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 119 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 205. Hyphenation with negative particles
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-,' 'in-,' and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen; the particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate; non-aesthetic, non-subservient, but: nonage, nondescript, nonessential.

rubrics_metrics.name: 206. 'Quasi-' requires hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi' prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 207. 'Over' and 'under' generally unhyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (lengthy words, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed; exceptions: over-soul, under-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: 208. Latin prepositional prefixes usually unhyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: The Latin prepositions 'ante,' 'anti,' 'inter,' 'intra,' 'post,' 'sub,' and 'super' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, international, postscript; exceptions like ante-bellum, anti-Semitic.

rubrics_metrics.name: 209. 'Extra/infra/supra/ultra' usually hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra,' 'infra,' 'supra,' and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: 210. Hyphenation in spelled-out fractional numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'two-thirds' 'four and five-sevenths' 'thirty-hundredths'; but don't hyphenate in constructions like 'one half of his fortune...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 211. Hyphen to indicate omitted common element in series of compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of two or more compound words occurring together which have one of their component elements in common and omitted from all but the last word, indicate the omission by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: 212. Hyphen to indicate prefix/suffix particle
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or a suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 213. Hyphen employed to indicate syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 214. Certain common words should be hyphenated (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescribed list of everyday words that should be hyphenated is provided (words that do not fall under earlier classifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the list: after-years, bas-relief, son-in-law, birth-rate, page-proof, title-page, well-being, cross-examine, guinea-pig, sea-level, sense-perception, will-power, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 215. Avoid unnecessary word divisions at line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words. Wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General typographic preference: minimize hyphenation and divisions when spacing allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: 216. Restrict dividing short syllables in wide measures; spacing paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, in wide measures (20 ems or more), divide on a syllable of two letters if possible; good spacing, however, is always paramount. Words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical hyphenation guidance for line breaks in wide measure text; prioritize spacing over rigid syllable-count rules.
